title: Two sisters checked into a cute English B&B. Then the key broke | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

In our roundup of travel stories this week: An American artist who paints Paris, clay tablets that illuminate life centuries ago, a “rescue” at a country inn, plus another CNN Postcard.

Sometimes vacations don’t go as planned. American sisters Jan and Jill Shropshire discovered this the hard way on a trip to the English Midlands in 1997.

A mistake with the key led to Jill accidentally locking the pair of them inside their room in a countryside B&B in a converted old house. Then when they tried to summon help, they realized they were all alone in the building.

They survived their ordeal and were eventuallyrescued, with thanks to some peanut butter, a free-standing sink and some helpful Russians.

Operating out of the rugged landscape of what is modern-day central Turkey, the Hittites were a powerhouse empire some 3,500 years ago. They raided Babylon, built an awesome fleet of armored chariots and squared up against legendary Egyptian pharaohs like Ramesses the Great.

They’ve been largely forgotten by popular history, but are now back in the headlines thanks to a startling discovery at Šamuḫa, an ancient dig site in central Turkey. Archaeologists recently unearthed a stash of cuneiform-inscribed clay tablets, which offer an intimate, and occasionally strange, peek intoeveryday life 35 centuries ago.

Exploring a city on foot is an unbeatable way to take the pulse of a new destination.

And some streets offer travelers a unique window on the local culture because they are “home to indie businesses, events or festivals you wouldn’t find elsewhere,” according to Time Out editor Grace Beard, who spoke to CNN Travel about the magazine’s annual ranking of the world’s coolest streets.

Among the streets highlighted on this year’s list are Song Wat Road in Bangkok and Montréal’s Boulevard Saint-Laurent in Canada.

You can see if your favorite streetmade the list.

A new feature has debuted: CNN Postcards. Brief but vivid stories capturing the wonder, joy, humor or drama of travel.

Visiting Mexico with our toddler, we took taxis around Isla Mujeres, an island off Cancun. Hailing a cab one evening, we found other passengers already aboard. But they said nothing, so we squeezed in, my son balanced on my lap.

We got used to sharing taxis. Then one day, a driver was accompanied by his family. With a stack of tortillas on the dashboard, his wife prepared beef tacos. She handed her husband a taco, then assembled one for her son.

I can still see the boy’s big, sleepy eyes, and the taco made on the dashboard of his father’s taxi. (Jeanne Bonner)

Most of the year, Bolivia’s Salar de Uyuni is a flat, white monolith. But come rainy season, the water collects in a sheet that blurs the line between earth and sky, creating a one-of-a-kind visual show.
